utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, good morning, everyone. Mr. O'Sullivan, there is an application before us for additional protective measures in relation to the next witness. Are counsel for the accused in a position to deal with this application now?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No objection. Now, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's an application to extend the protective measures for this witness which I just want to be clear about -- on which I want to be clear about one thing. An application was made in July when you would expect any problems that had been experienced would have been resolved. And here we have an application made today which is going to cost the loss of another half-hour of time, if it's granted, because we will have to adjourn while the arrangement is put in place. It's another example of the disturbance of the schedule, which is caused by Prosecution proofing at the last minute. And we are becoming increasingly anxious that something's going to have to be done about this to prevent these situations from arising at the last minute. The disturbance to the schedule is caused, first of all, by the delivery of information late to the Defence; and secondly, by giving rise to the need for loss of time while technical arrangements are put in place. Now, is there nothing that can be done to carry out this proofing exercise at an earlier stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- what can be done, generally speaking, is to bring the witnesses earlier, which would involve significant additional resource outlays or, as is done in this case, to go to the witness, which again involves significant outlays if it had to be done in respect of every witness. We -- there's nothing else I could suggest. We do try and we could try even more when it comes to protective measures to contact the witnesses by telephone or by some other means, by officers in the field, to get clear information. But there are just occasions which are sometimes inescapable when we hear the information at the last minute, as in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's a useful suggestion, that contact should be made by telephone earlier. The one other thing -- the two are related but the thing I really want to be clear about is why this problem didn't emerge in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, in July he did not mention and he was not asked -- well, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The situation is a developing situation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just hold on a second. We'll go into private session for this because I want to discuss the previous protective measures.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I simply confirm, so that there's no doubt as far as the public is concerned, that the application for additional protective measures has been granted and the witness will give evidence with his voice also distorted. So we shall adjourn and resume at ten minutes to 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, with the indulgence of the interpreters, we will now sit until 11.30, have a half-hour break, and then we'll sit from 12.00 to 1.45, so that way we will recoup some of the time that's been lost this morning. Mr. Stamp, the next witness is K-82?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: K-82, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning. K-82, can you hear me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just a second, I'll deal with the declaration first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Complete the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the witness does not have the -- yeah. Sir, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He just took the solemn declaration. I think he was prompted by the registrar there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please be seated. Now, Mr. Stamp, help me, how is the sound transmitted? Is it through one of these open telephone call --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think it's by way of a conference call machine there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm surprised he doesn't have earphones, but they're not required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Witness K-82, you're about to be asked questions by a number of counsel, first of all representing the Prosecution and then representing the various accused here. They will be asking questions to either add to or explain or even challenge evidence which we already have before us. The Judges already have copies of a fairly detailed statement that you've given, and the important thing is that in answering questions today you pay close attention to the question that's being asked and deal with the particular issue that's raised in the question. There's no point in repeating what we already have before us in your statement. So please listen carefully to each question and give an answer confined to the point that the question relates to. And the first person to question you will be for the Prosecution, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning again, K-82, and in the course of your testimony we'll refer to you as "K-82." Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-82
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like first to show you a document, and I want you to look at it, read it, and say whether or not the document describes you personally. Do not read it aloud.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P2302?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] K-82.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I must hear everything that's going on. It's not appropriate to switch off the sound. Now, what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness K-82, you see that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-82
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Does --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-82
utterances.text: Yes, I see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd really like to know what the registrar was telling the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, so would I. What was happening there? I can't hear anything that's happening. I can hear the witness when he -- when he's translated, but I can't hear what the registrar is saying.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] -- loud, therefore I just closed it. Can you hear me, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While we're waiting, Your Honour, could I hand a copy of Exhibit 2302 so that we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, you can hand a copy to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I believe the Defence already has copies of this document. It's a pseudonym sheet and it's in e-court. Can I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm still waiting for the explanation from the registrar as to what was going on in the court, in the room. Why can't she speak to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you just speak using the same system that the witness just spoke through to tell us what happened at the point when you first showed him the pseudonym sheet?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can't hear that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] Can you hear me, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, now I can.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] Your Honour, sorry, but the witness was about to read it aloud; therefore, I just -- I closed it in order not to make him read it out loud. That's the only reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Sarajevo] You're welcome, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Stamp, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: K-82, does that document contain accurate personal information about yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P2315, which is his statement dated the 14th of September, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: K-82, on the 14th of September, 2006, did you give a statement to the Prosecution or to officers of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And is that a copy of it in front of you there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that statement you gave, was it read over to you at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-82
utterances.text: Yes, it was read back to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And is the statement true and accurate -- is it a true and accurate reflection of the evidence you would give? In other words, if you're asked questions about the matters stated therein now, would your answers remain the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-82
utterances.text: Yes. This statement I gave was read back to me and it is correct. The statement I have before me, as far as I can see, is in English, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On the English copy that you have in front of you, do you see where you have signed to it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in that statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what's -- what is the witness telling us? That he remembers it being read to him and that was accurate; is that the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And he doesn't have before him a B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He should. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, would it not be better to have him read one over before today to make sure that the B/C/S was a correct account? Has that been done?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness, do you see, along with the English version, a copy of the statement in B/C/S, in Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-82
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity of reading that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-82
utterances.text: Yes. This statement was read back to me by the interpreter once I had given it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is an English statement was translated and read over to you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you signed that statement, acknowledging the accuracy of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the statement describes primarily the activities of your military unit in Kosovo in 1999. Attached to the statement did you also mark three maps showing the places where your unit was involved in the various activities that you describe in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-82
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness K-82, I'd like you to remember that we have your statement so I'm only going to refer to some parts of it and just ask a couple questions for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but if the statement is being tendered I do have to make one short objection with respect to the portion contained in paragraph 31 which references the PJP which was not previously disclosed or contained in either of the six -- the witness notification, the prior statement, or in the extensive Milosevic testimony. There was no reference to any testimony relating to the PJP, so if the Prosecutor is going to lead any evidence on that I would be objecting to that portion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, he has led evidence by presenting the statement. Are you objecting to the references within the written paragraph 31?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's why I rise now rather than waiting for him to elicit live testimony in this regard. Because I understand the statement is being tendered pursuant to Rule 89(F) and I view the matters alleged at paragraph 31 to be improper based on the grounds that I've stated, limited to the PJP aspect, Your Honour, since that's the only part that I saw that was not previously disclosed or in the notification which -- to the contrary, the notification identifies that there were three companies of soldiers and that there were no -- I mean, it doesn't state that there were PJP present at all. So that's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's also reference in that paragraph to MUP reports, but they were disclosed to you, were they?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The MUP reports were in on e-court since last week, the first reference to PJP was in this statement which we received Friday evening. I don't know when the MUP reports exactly were disclosed, but I believe the reports themselves were disclosed previously; I just don't know whether they were linked to this particular witness. But I was aware of them, so I'm less concerned with them and more concerned with any testimony to be led with regard to the PJP which was not evident anywhere and will of course increase the questioning that I will do, which was going to be very limited based on the previous I have had hand and was previously given notice of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp, on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reference to the PJP is in fact an elaboration and a clarification of his previous given evidence and statements in respect to the movement of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What did he say before -- or who did he say before was responsible for moving them?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't believe he identified the persons before. He says was responsible for the bodies, but this is a situation where he says he merely believes or thought it must have been the PJP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you leading any oral evidence from him on this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you mean do I need to ask on what basis did he think or say it was the PJP? Your Honour, I would submit that the real issue is an issue of notice. And while it is ideal that in a summary or in previous testimony every single item that a witness may say upon elaboration is clearly notified. It is, nevertheless, possible that on later testimony there might be an elaboration in which there are asked slight --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there's a difference between an elaboration and a mentioning of an organisation for the first time. Mr. Ivetic's point is that he's got no notice -- until recently, that it's being suggested that the PJP were involved. And the way it's presented here, if we were to give this any credence at all, would suggest that the PJP were working in collaboration with the VJ in this operation. Now, that's a pretty significant matter, in my opinion, in this trial. And do you see it differently?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, I think it is significant, which is to some degree why I will ask one question about it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it's bringing in the PJP in his evidence for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That -- that, Your Honour, is something I would prefer to address more -- with more precision if I was given a little bit more time. I think it's something that could wait until after the break. But could I ask one moment to consult --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not at the moment, no, let us consider that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We take the view that this is a -- is not an elaboration of previous evidence, but this is a new account of events. As it stands, we would find it very difficult to give much weight to this, as suggesting that the PJP were involved, and we are not prepared to allow you to elaborate upon it since the Defence for the sixth accused are not in a position prior to cross-examining the witness to investigate the circumstances of the PJP at that time to conduct an adequate cross-examination. And therefore, we will exclude from consideration any reference to the PJP referred to in paragraph 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness, in -- Witness K-82, in paragraph 11 of your statement you told us about an operation that your unit was involved in, in the village of Trnje in the latter part of March 1999, and you said that around 80 -- I'm sorry, this is paragraph 10, 80 to 100 soldiers were involved in this operation and that you arrived on a hill overlooking the village and sometime earlier that morning Captain Gavrilovic, the battalion commander, gave an order to the sergeants, sergeants who were in charge of some platoons of your unit. Can you recall what the order was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K-82
utterances.text: Yes, I can. He turned to the sergeants and he asked whether companies were ready for action. They answered positively. After that, he turned towards the village and pointed at it with his hand, and he said: "There is no one to be left there." And once the sergeants understood what he said, they turned back to their companies, they assembled, and they headed off towards the village. The first two companies were led by Kozlina and Nedeljkovic, whereas Fejzic remained on the hill with his company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can -- I should have had you tell us which paragraphs of the indictment this statement relates to. This particular incident is in which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is not a scheduled incident in the sense that it is not narrated in any of the paragraphs of the indictment. But evidence relates to paragraphs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, this is a very specific event you're talking about. It's not in the indictment and it's in March 1999? Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why is it not in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I asked a similar question and there were at times past opportunities when the indictment was being amended to include it. The evidence, I am told, came to attention sometime after the indictment was proffered, sometime -- just about the close of the Kosovo part in the Milosevic trial. And the opportunities to amend it, although they existed, there were different or varying considerations. And it was thought that the indictment, having made allegations or allegations to matters and events that occurred in Kosovo leading to the movement of the population, not all incidents that came to our attention in the course of preparing the case needed to be included in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So why do you include any then? I mean, what is the rationale of an indictment? Is it not supposed to set out the detailed events that are going to be the subject of evidence, particularly the ones between January and June 1989 [sic]?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed it is. The specific incidents in the indictment is paragraphs 72 and 75 are illustrations of a general course of conduct, a widespread and systematic course of conduct carried out by the force of FRY and Serbia at that period. Now, the indictment was proffered I think in 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it was a --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And various incidents have come to our attention after that. The Prosecution would be in a position to have to make a decision. Do we take out an incident and add one or do we add more illustrations? And it might well reach a point when the indictment would be overloaded with illustrations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So I think the decision was made earlier -- it was a judgement call that was made earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I now do not understand what this indictment actually tells us. It just tells us about the incidents you think you should specify and it doesn't tell us about the other ones, no matter how specific they are, if you've decided not to specify them. Is that how I have to read the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, the indictment does in many paragraphs refer to the general widespread and systematic course of conduct similar or descriptive of this particular incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But surely that is a conclusion that we are invited to reach, having made particular findings on the specific crimes set out in individual paragraphs of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. So you would expect this one that you're now dealing with to be a paragraph in the indictment, among many others, from which we would draw the conclusion if we found them established that the conduct was widespread and systematic. But instead you're telling me: There might be an endless number of incidents of significance that aren't mentioned in here. And because you've talked of conduct being widespread and systematic, that entitles you to lead evidence about anything that happened in Kosovo at any time within the time period?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Well, tell me where I've misunderstood then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The indictment charges widespread and systematic conduct against Kosovar Albanians by the forces of the FRY. Various paragraphs of the indictment tell us quite clearly what that conduct amounted to. Specific illustrations are given in the indictment; them being illustrations, they can only be of limited number. The indictment having been proffered other, shall I say, outstanding illustrations of the conduct pleaded in the indictment may come to the attention of the Prosecution. And those specific instances come under the general pleadings in the indictment in respect to conduct throughout Kosovo which led to the population movement. So the issue really is whether or not the Prosecution must plead every single incident specifically. I would submit not. But it does not mean that everything that happened in Kosovo becomes provable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, tell me something would not -- you wouldn't be able to lead evidence about. Give me an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Crimes -- crimes committed by persons not being part of the force of the FRY or Serbia as charged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Assuming it was something done by the army, tell me something that you would not be able to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Crimes committed in such a manner that they do not indicate or that it is not of reasonable inference that they were intended to create a climate of fear and to expel the population. These crimes clearly fall within the ambit of the general crime described in the indictment, the burning of the houses while the population was expelled, the killing of the people in public, the shooting at people, at crowds of people when they descended into the town, the random murder, but particularly the destruction of the people's houses. These are the types of crimes that were generally described in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are there other events in here that are not in this statement that are not mentioned in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Or is it only this particular event? Are there other events in this witness's statement not referred to in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, not specifically referred in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And which are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There is an incident at Ljubizda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's paragraph 5 in December 1998. That is more relevant to the background. There is an incident at Jeskovo in February 1999 related to the background of the events we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, paragraph 5. Which others?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The second incident I mentioned is paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There is an incident at the village of Mamusa in paragraph 27, and Rogovo in paragraph 34. All of these are offences referable to Prizren or the municipality of Prizren where we charge persecution and the relevant indictment paragraphs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And if you were to take this to its logical conclusion, accused could be convicted on the basis of this evidence alone in this court, even though no mention is made in the indictment of the events in these various paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: They --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what you would say, that you could be convicted here on an indictment that doesn't even mention the things that you're convicted of?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would not submit at this point that you could be convicted of this alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Prosecution's case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why could there not be a murder conviction arising out of the events in this statement alone, events that aren't mentioned in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, in a general sense there could be a conviction, but in respect to the indictment for the court, not. I would, without having had the opportunity to fully advise myself, I would submit that these allegations, if proven, in conjunction with the specific illustrations set out in the indictment would be sufficient or could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, let's assume there's an acquittal of all the others that are specified in the indictment. You could be convicted on the strength of these ones alone?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is a submission which I probably would like to make if I advise myself fully on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I should tell Your Honour that I discussed the very issue you're talking about with some of my colleagues yesterday because I noticed that no incident this person describes is contained in the indictment. And it was my understanding that there was a previous witness that testified here before I came who testified about an incident not contained in the indictment, and his testimony was permitted because it went to the issue of widespread and systematic but that the specific incident itself could not be the basis of any conviction. That was my understanding, even though I didn't go read the ruling Your Honour made at that point. I now hear the Prosecutor saying that even though we've not been given indictment notice of these events, that it's his position that you could convict us based upon these events and I think that's a bit startling on the jurisprudence in this Tribunal. And if that's the basis on which it's being offered, then I should strongly object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we are going to adjourn to consider this. K-82, I greatly regret that we've got involved in a legal argument while hearing your evidence, but it's a matter of some importance and the Trial Chamber will need to take some time to consider how it's going to address this issue. It may be that some further submissions are required before we can make any determination of it, but we need to at least give it some preliminary consideration. Regrettably we were not given this statement. I don't know why, but we didn't have it until this morning and therefore everything has happened rather quickly. So we will alert you when you're ready to resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, thank you for your patience. The first thing I ought to make clear is that -- well, sorry, Mr. Stamp, do you have something to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was wondering if I could bring to the attention of the Court one or two submissions particularly in respect to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, you'll have an opportunity in a moment. The first thing I want to do is make it clear that we will not require the witness for the rest of today. So there is no point in the witness remaining in the room where the broadcast is coming from. He should be available tomorrow, but whether we need him depends on what we decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, second piece of clarification that's initially required is whether we can conduct this debate now in open session. I do want to feel free to refer to the localities that are the subject of the debate. Does that present any problem? I don't think it does because the evidence was going to be heard. So it would appear to me there's no reason why we shouldn't be in open session. I hear no one disagreeing with that, so we shall conduct the proceedings now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stamp, I would like you to clarify certain things to help us understand where you say the indictment allows this evidence to be led. If you take, first of all, paragraph 11 was the -- was the paragraph that you were dealing with first of all. And that leads on to other paragraphs which describe events in more detail. Now, how do you say that that evidence could be said to be relevant to the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Paragraph 11 is a paragraph in which we have a senior officer of the VJ giving an order which we would later submit whether he had something now as an order which can be interpreted to the one -- to the troops to go into the town and commit crimes. The following paragraphs in the indictment -- in the statement describe these crimes, the burning and destruction of houses and other property, the indiscriminate shooting, the murder of civilians, and generally the creation of a climate of fear which caused the civilians to flee the town. These facts are specifically relevant to paragraphs -- I think it's 23 to 32 of the indictment. In fact, paragraph 5, paragraph 25, dealing with expulsion -- and the -- now the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, that -- these paragraphs are an overview of the joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is the heading, but the paragraph -- these paragraphs describe the conduct -- the conduct of the force of the FRY who carried out the aims and purposes of the joint criminal enterprise. Paragraph 25, expulsion; paragraph 26, the destruction and burning; paragraph 27, violence and threats against civilian population; paragraph 30, looting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is a general narrative of the joint criminal enterprise. That's the heading and that, I assume, is what it's meant to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is a narrative of the conduct of the force of the FRY and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As part of?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As part of the effecting of the joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It -- when you look at that evidence in conjunction with two of the exhibits towards the documents exhibited in this statement, you will see that those documents show that the forces of the FRY and Serbia in this particular case with particular -- with -- particular to the VJ were engaged in an operation in that area. I should not just say the VJ but the brigade that this witness was a member of. That is the 549 Motorised Brigade. 24th, 25th, 26th, 27th of March in the areas of Orahovac, Suva Reka, Mala Krusa, Bela Crkva, and also Trnje. Inside witnesses are difficult to get, so we have no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a separate matter entirely. Whether it's difficult to get or not has absolutely nothing to do with whether what he says is relevant to the indictment. The fact that you have someone in a hot seat in a court who can tell you something that sounds like a crime doesn't mean it fits in the indictment. Let's concentrate on the argument how the evidence is relevant to the indictment. Now, which municipality is Trnovo in, for example -- sorry, Trnje I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Prizren municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Prizren. Now, we've got events in Prizren in counts 1 and 2 I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Counts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Paragraph 72.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Paragraph 72, paragraph 75 I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't think you'll find it in 75, which is the murder paragraph. We don't have any murders in Prizren, I don't think. But please correct me if I'm wrong. I know it's sometimes very difficult to follow everything that's averred.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, we do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So how do we get these killings into this indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- which is precisely what I was getting to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- when I referred to him being an insider witness. We have no insiders for specifically Velika Krusa, Mala Krusa, Suva Reka, maybe one in respect to Suva Reka, but not a witness to the killings. We have a document which shows that these offences of the 25th, 24th, 26th -- well, I should say the 23rd to the 28th of March in that -- in the brigade area of responsibility were committed by his unit of that brigade in a particular area. So it identifies brigade members of being involved in that type of conduct. The murders at Velika Krusa, Mala Krusa, and other areas -- or Orahovac, if I have the pronunciation right, are in the area of responsibility of which this soldier as a member or this ex-soldier as a member. So his testimony touches directly on the course of conduct, the pattern of conduct, of the brigade whose area of operation involved those -- that particular part of Kosovo. So it assists to identify participants in the crimes mentioned in paragraphs 32, 24 to 32, 72, and 75 in particular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, paragraph -- these are the -- are these paragraphs of the indictment you're mentioning?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have lost me here, I must say. This witness is going to talk of events in Velika Krusa, Mala Krusa, Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, he will not speak of those events, but his brigade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Then, how does that -- how does the fact that he can speak to events in another municipality impact on behaviour in these ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He speaks of events in which his brigade, the brigade that he is a member of, participated in. These events signify or these are events from which the Court, the trier of fact, can make inferences, A, not only in terms of the widespread and systematic element of the offences with which he is charged -- or with which the accused are charged, but also in respect of the conduct of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So if it commits murder in one municipality, it must inevitably be committing murder somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Not inevitably, Your Honour. The Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, is it not traditionally the case in criminal law that you don't infer that a person will murder in one place because he's committed a murder somewhere else? We actually expect evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We're speaking about an organisation here, Your Honour, not a person. We are speaking about the brigade of which this accused is a member of. We're saying that the evidence shows what the brigade -- the conduct of the brigade in general in its area of responsibility and the command apparatus in respect of punishing persons or not -- who would not participate in that -- in the crimes that are charged in the indictment. I had indicated that there were a couple precedents that I wished to refer the Court to. One which is on point with what I was just describing is from the Kupreskic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you go to that, are you therefore saying you would not in this case seek a conviction for murder in Trnje, that would never happen; all you would do is seek to invite the Chamber to draw an inference about behaviour in municipalities where charges do exist in the indictment from the way in which this brigade behaved in Trnje and the other places that we may yet come on to in this discussion?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we would not submit and we do not submit that a conviction for these particular villages would be appropriate. However, the evidence in respect to these particular villages, for a variety of reasons, can support a conviction on those offences which involve the widespread and systematic nature of the charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's a very vague answer, if I may say so, because it can mean two separate things. Are you saying that the crimes on which you will seek convictions are limited to the specific ones set out in the subparagraphs of, for example, paragraph 72?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that when you re-incorporate these general allegations in the various paragraphs you've been referring to earlier in the indictment, you re-incorporate them at paragraph 71. There you re-incorporate paragraphs 60 to 69. You will not seek convictions in respect of these particular -- of any crimes based on the generality of the allegations in these paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that does clarify something about which we have been extremely concerned for some time and it leaves an outstanding matter which I don't think we need to deal with at this particular stage. Now, you were going to go on to authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I pause here to indicate that the authorities on the matter seem to me to be to manifold and seem to aim in one direction. When it comes to authorities I suggest, and it was just a suggestion, that perhaps the Court might well benefit from written submissions perhaps delivered today, later on today, since we are sitting in the afternoon tomorrow. However, without having the authorities here I could cite some of them quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The first is from the Kupreskic appeals decision. And the -- I'm sorry, I don't yet have the paragraph number for the passage I wish to quote which reads: "The Appeals Chamber, however, finds that Witness DD's testimony concerning Josipovic's presence at Ahmic house may still be considered as corroborating evidence for the determination of Josipovic's involvement in the offence that was set out in the Amended Indictment, that is the attack on Musafer Puscul's house. Support for this position can be found in Rule 93 of the Rules, which allows for the admission of evidence of a consistent pattern of conduct relevant to serious violations of international humanitarian law in the interests of justice. Similarly, under the so-called principle of 'similar fact evidence,' courts in England and Wales, Australia, and the United States admit evidence of crimes of wrongful acts committed by the defendant other than those charged in the indictment, if the other crimes are introduced to demonstrate a special knowledge, opportunity, or identification of the defendant that would make it more likely that he committed the instant crime as well." This is from the Kupreskic Appeals Chamber decision, and it's paragraph 321 I am told. The Strugar decision of the 22nd of January, 19 -- 22nd of January, 2002 on the Defence's objection to the Prosecution opening statement concerning admissibility of evidence was to the effect that courts will generally admit evidence of acts of the accused other than those charged in the indictment, provided that this evidence is used to prove an issue relevant to the charge, such as motive, opportunity, intent, preparation, plan, or knowledge. And this decision was also quoted in the -- I think all of them were approved -- these decisions were approved in the aforementioned Strugar case where it was also said - and this is the penultimate reference I will make - it was also said at paragraph 323, considering that a review of the practice in national jurisdictions shows that: "Courts will generally admit evidence of acts of the accused other than those charged in the indictment, provided that this evidence is used to prove an issue relevant to the charges, such as motive, opportunity, intent, preparation, plan, or knowledge." And it made specific reference to the federal rules of evidence for United States courts. The -- another decision which I would like to comment on, and it's a last citation I will make, and that's the decision in the -- that's a judgement in the Galic case delivered on the 5th of December, 2003, at paragraph 186. I think it's paragraph 185 to 191 which would be relevant, and that -- those paragraphs are under the general rubric evaluation of evidence. In the -- in paragraphs 186 to 188 they refer to what were in that case called a -- scheduled incidents, which for these purposes are the same as those incidents which we specifically describe in paragraphs 72 and 75 of this incident. In the Galic indictment the difference is that they put them in schedules to the indictment. They were called scheduled sniping incidents and scheduled shelling incidents. In that case the Prosecution led evidence to prove a variety of matters including the widespread and systematic nature of the offence and in reference to those non-scheduled offences or in reference to the evidence of those non-scheduled evidence the Trial Chamber said at paragraph 189: "At the same time, the Trial Chamber has given no less attention to evidence of non-scheduled sniping and shelling incidents as well as to evidence of other aspects of the situation in Sarajevo. The scheduled incidents have thus been considered by the Trial Chamber within a more general evidentiary context, reflecting how the greater number of witnesses in the case understood them and explained them. Witnesses' -- witness evidence together with documentary evidence has been chosen, combined, and arranged with the Trial Chamber in accordance with its relevance, the credibility of its source, and its probative value, with due regard to the fact that the present Indictment alleges unlawful conduct and responsibility for such conduct going beyond what is referred to in the scheduled incidents." Those are the words that I'd like to emphasise. The Prosecution's case here, as is clear I think, goes beyond the incidents charged within the indictment. Those are the authorities. I think I could deal with them more carefully and with more precise citations if we were permitted time to furnish a written submission. The -- I don't know if Your Honour wants to restrict my response now to that part, the incidents at Trnovo -- Trnje, because there are other areas of this witness's statement which are relevant to the allegations in the indictment, including relation to 7(3), that is Article 7(3) within this corps -- within this -- the Pristina Corps, the brigade in question that this soldier was a member of, soldiers who refused to participate were threatened. That course of conduct is relevant to the Court's consideration, it is my respectful submission, of 7(3) issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't dispute that it would be relevant to 7(3) issues. My question is: Is it relevant to the indictment? That's what you have to concentrate on. All of your evidence is relevant in a general sense, it's relevant to events in Kosovo. The question for us is whether it's relevant to this indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- in respect to the 7(3) aspect, for example, the evidence of the burying of the bodies, for example, goes to a variety of passages in the indictment, where it is alleged that instead of taking corrective action to prevent or punish these crimes, systems were put in place for the concealment of the evidence, for the concealment of the bodies. So when this witness refers to his brigade being involved in that, that evidence is relevant to the various parts of the indictment dealing with concealment of bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give me an example where there's a reference to concealment of bodies in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Paragraph 41(g) and the same allegation is made I think in pretty much the same formula with the same formula in respect to the other accused. That paragraph I just mentioned, which was to the accused General Ojdanic. It's used in respect to other accused in paragraphs 46(e), to the accused Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there then an averment to the steps that were taken to conceal bodies?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not ... The evidence speaks to a system in place for the concealment of bodies and the -- the indictment -- the averments in the indictment refer to the planning for the concealment of bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you where we see that one of the things that was planned was the concealment of bodies. It's a simple thing to state in an indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There is reference that in respect to Suva Reka, that is 75(d), paragraph 75(d).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: See, I thought that was what the purpose of the indictment was, so that you could set out examples like this as the ones that evidence would be led about and we would all know where we stood, what we were supposed to be judging. That's a perfectly sensible averment there, and no doubt you will try by evidence to link it with paragraph 41(g). But it still remains unclear to me at the moment why that simple course wasn't followed and these specific events were not included in the appropriate paragraphs of 72 and 75 so that we know exactly what it is we are to return verdicts on. But at least in relation to 72 you've told me -- and I assume the same applies to 75 - that you would not seek verdicts of the commission of crimes in relation to the events that are pled here -- in relation to the events that are not pled in the indictment. Now, I was going to ask you, Mr. Stamp, about paragraph 5, how it fits into the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I believe that the issue as to the admissibility of evidence in respect to 1998 was decided by this Court before, so I don't want to say anything that might not be consistent with the weight of that because -- I would say this, that there is -- that in this case, as in any other case, the background, the development of the events, the leading up to the precise charges which are before the Court may be important to the Court in deciding issues that joint criminal enterprise and the participants, issues like motive, issues like intent. The evidence in paragraph 5 relates to matters specifically discussed in the indictment in respect to 1998 and in the pre-trial brief as well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This particular --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Not this particular piece --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This particular operation?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Not the particular operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's why -- see, we were actually -- we went through an amendment process in which we had to consider whether it was reasonable for you to lead evidence about 1998, and you specified a number of events. And in light of that and our overall assessment of the relevance of that, we decided to allow amendment, and it's surprising you don't include all the ones that you want to lead evidence about at the stage you're amending the indictment. And therefore, I -- I'm surprised that we come across one here that's not mentioned there. And its relevance you say is what?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The situation as it developed to Racak in January, the Rambouillet meetings in February, and eventually the NATO -- the action by NATO and most of the offences charged in the indictment between February and June 1999 are relevant matters of joint criminal enterprise when it begun, who the participants were, relevant to the motive which we charge in the indictment or the intent or purpose of joint criminal enterprise. It shows that they -- that notwithstanding the ostensible or averred comportment by the force of the FRY, that is that they comported with the agreement with the OSCE in respect to the use of force in 1998. It shows that they did not. It shows that there was a course of conduct which predated the specific period in the indictment and which led to and culminated in the incidents that we are specifically engaged with here in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, there's too much background noise typing and we're having difficulties. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't understand what you've just said. I understand -- a course of conduct indicating the development of a joint criminal enterprise or at least evidence indicating that the accused were aware of what was happening and either were responsible for organising and planning it or otherwise for executing it. But I understood that in paragraph 95 you had set out the events that you would actually lead evidence about to show this, 94 and 95, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, these are specific references to specific incidents as pled and I still respectfully submit that the formula used in these two paragraphs indicate that these are not exclusively the incidents that relate to those occurrences in 1998, that the case goes well beyond those specifically cited incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the other paragraph -- paragraph 6 was one, how does that manage to escape the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As I indicated, Your Honour, there are -- it is not possible to put in the indictment specific incidents. All important matters that the Prosecution intends to lead evidence about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a frightening proposition because we don't have time for that trial, Mr. Stamp. We have time for this trial that's down here. Are you telling me that the number of other events that you will lead evidence about exceeds the number that are specified in the indictment at present?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I mean exceed -- you may have, I don't know, you may have 30 or 40 incidents referred to. Are you going to tell me that you're going to be leading evidence about more -- another 50, say, on top of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I wouldn't go so far as to say 50, but insofar as evidence of an event is relevant to the various matters at issue in the court, then it is our submission that it is admissible. I don't want to go as far as to say that it can be controlled by the various provisions of the Rules which entitle the court to control the amount of evidence. But in terms of the issue of admissibility, once it is relevant to the live issues -- relevant and probative to the live issues, it is our submission that even if it is not a specifically pleaded event, then it's admissible. The concern, of course, which is expressed by the Court is that then the -- there would be no control over the length of the trial and what the trial covers, but there are other provisions in the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But this particular one you referred to says: "I think 25 to 30 people were killed in that operation and he saw the bodies of those people. Now, that doesn't warrant a mention in the indictment. So no one's being prosecuted -- no one here's being prosecuted for that event. The Prosecution have chosen not to prosecute that event. Is that the position. And Ms. Moeller laughs, but I'd like to know the answer to that. Has the Prosecution decided: We do not seek a conviction for that particular killing? Because the story we constantly hear in general terms from the Prosecution is they must fill an indictment with specific allegations of crimes because the people of Kosovo expect that these crimes will be recognised in the judgements of the Tribunal. But here you tell me now that you don't even mention an incident in the indictment, you don't prosecute on the basis that you will seek a conviction for it, but you now want to bring it in, in some other basis. Now, I think that these comments are inconsistent with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There's a balance that we have to draw as Prosecutors. I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You know, at this moment, I don't actually think you've thought about it as Prosecutors. That's the impression I'm getting, that it's something you've decided latterly to bring in. When you were doing the amendment process, at the moment my impression is you didn't think of this. Now, convince me I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- there have been more than one amendment processes. The evidence came to the attention of the Prosecution in 2002, in the middle of that year, three years also after the -- this indictment was proffered. When such incidents are brought to the attention of Prosecution, there is at that stage a decision to be made. The Prosecution has always submitted that we try in the indictments to have illustrations with the specific events, but it is impossible for us to put in the indictment every single event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I accept that. But it's for you to choose which ones to put in, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And to prosecute for them. And hard decisions have to be taken. You can't prosecute for everything, but you can't surely come along later and say: Well, we made that decision but now we're going to bring it in by the backdoor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We -- the backdoor, I'm not sure if that is entirely the course we are adopting. We would lead in respect to the incidents, scheduled incidents, we would lead as much as we can with certainly a significant amount of evidence on these incidents, on what occurred to the persons. We have quite a number of witnesses who prove, it is our submission, these incidents. Here we have a witness who describes other incidents which could be scheduled if it is admitted. But should we add another incident to the -- the many -- the dozens of incidents already on the indictment, that's a call that was made and the call was that we would go according -- and this is what I've been told, that we'd go according to what the law provided -- our interpretation of the law. And that it is relevant to prove a variety of matters, in particular the organisation and conduct of the brigade which -- whose area of operation was where many of the incidents in the indictment were committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, the -- whose area of operation --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Included --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't even mention this brigade in the indictment, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't think brigades are specifically mentioned in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We called several times for specification of the units involved in the various operations, tried to get you to identify them over a long period of time. And I think they're identified in general terms, but I don't think you referred to specific brigade -- a specific brigade carrying out this operation -- or operations in particular areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am confident --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm learning a great deal today, Mr. Stamp, that causes me great concern about the future of this case. I'm -- I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can't believe something you said earlier and I just want to verify it. Are you saying that you are going to attempt to lead evidence about incidents not referred to -- crime bases not referred to in the indictment which may together exceed the number of crime bases that are already referred to in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is not the intention of the Prosecution to lead evidence of incidents that exceed the number already in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I thought you said earlier that you did, and I've obviously misunderstood or somebody's misunderstood somebody there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I did, I apologise, which is probably it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to identify how many more of these are likely to come across.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The evidence as it stands now, I could address that specifically given an opportunity to address some of these issues in writing. And I do understand the concern of the Court about how do you maintain control of a trial. And I say this not to encourage the Court to use those provisions to maintain control as to the size of a trial. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, going back --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The real issue here is an issue of admissibility, if the question is put simply, is the extent to which nonscheduled incidents are relevant, are relevant and probative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Going back then to the specific, what is it you say paragraph 6 goes to? Is it the same sort of thing or is there something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- it goes to what I previously outlined in respect to the course of conduct of the force of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Contrary to claims they were acting in accordance with international agreements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is that the same as 27 and 34?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think these are paragraphs that relate to matters that again go to show the widespread and systematic nature of the campaign, as alleged in the indictment in various places. The events referred to in paragraphs 27 and 34 -- 27, to be specific, would be a paragraph that is relevant to paragraph 99 of the indictment and also paragraph 30 -- 30 and 26, 26 which deals with destruction of the property of Kosovar Albanians in a general sense, looting, and robbery in paragraph 30 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, the way I read these averments of joint criminal enterprise was as a general statement narrative of events which were then specified in paragraphs 72 and 75 in particular. I didn't read them initially certainly as carte blanche to lead evidence of anything that happened in Kosovo that might be described as deportation or murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the Prosecution is not submitting that, Your Honour. We submit that the -- this evidence not only is evidence of the widespread and systematic pattern that we claim in the indictment, but it shows -- it's evidence from what the Court can make reasonable inferences as to the perpetrators, reasonable inference to the system in place for planning, reasonable inferences as to the system or lack of system for prevention of a crime or punishment of perpetrators, reasonable inferences in respect to how the organisation -- not individually, the organisation that the accused commanded, treated dissident persons, persons who committed crimes, reasonable inference about how the organisation attempted to conceal the evidence in respect to these crimes. So it does touch upon an event which is not in the indictment, and certainly I suspect if we included it in the indictment or attempted to add it to the indictment, we might well have been -- the Defence, I'm sure, might well have objected strenuously to another specific count on which they could be convicted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'll have to re-read what was said at the time of the amendment, but my recollection was that you couldn't be more specific about what various groups of the army were doing, and now I find it quite frightening to hear that in 2002 you were aware of this systematic way of behaviour of a particular brigade and it's never featured in the indictment to alert us, the Trial Bench, if no one else, to how you were actually going to present your case. Now, anything else to be submitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I have no further submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Although I would ask that you consider the suggestion I made in respect to written submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As far as your running order of witnesses is concerned, will you have another witness available tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is unlikely. We did -- and we are making -- taking steps to ensure that there is always somebody waiting, but at this point in time we don't have anyone waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Wednesday, will there be other witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Wednesday I think we will have witnesses available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan, do you wish to submit anything on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, I think my submissions would be limited to submissions on behalf of Mr. Milutinovic. My colleagues may want to supplement after I'm through. There is -- I'm sure the Chamber is anxious to resolve this matter, as we are, but there is some important case law that was cited by the Prosecution and I invite the Bench to review the Kupreskic Appeals Chamber decision, that's the leading jurisprudence on indictments and defects in an indictment, notice, and the corollary issue of relevance at trial. And we say that the core issue here is in fact the indictment as the charging instrument which puts us on notice on the case we must meet, with the corollary of relevance of the evidence at trial. Now, we have examples here of the -- as it was pointed out in your exchange with Mr. Stamp that the general narrative of our indictment is specified by the five counts, and the five counts are what has put us on notice. And that is the relevant -- those are the relevant matters on which -- and only on which evidence can be led. I must take issue with the Prosecution because they cannot be heard to say that since the first Milosevic and other indictment of 1999 and the severance to the first Milutinovic joint indictment and then the Pavkovic joint indictment of 2003 and then our joinder indictment of this year that they have not been aware of other relevant matters which could have been charged and that is the fundamental flaw, we say, in their submission. As well, I would like the Chamber to look at the Strugar and Galic indictments and the case law referred to by my learned friend. In Strugar in particular that case deals with the acts of an accused other than those charged against him. It's the acts of the accused. In our indictment, our clients are charged with commission through participation in a JCE, not as the perpetrators of offences. Strugar is different. It's distinguishable on that ground. Now, I will repeat that the Kupreskic jurisprudence, which I cannot at this moment off the top of my head go into in great detail, but it is the leading jurisprudence on indictments and this is the very issue of notice, both through the indictment and the pre-trial brief, of which we've had two in this case, before joinder and after joinder, has put us on notice to the case we must meet. And this is not being fulfilled and it leads to an issue of the fundamental fairness of this trial. Those are the matters I wish to state at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: May I add to that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, Mr. Sepenuk, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Just following on with what Mr. O'Sullivan said, let's just assume for the moment that Mr. Stamp is correct, whatever written submissions he submits to you satisfies you that the evidence has the probative value Mr. Stamp says it has, meaning it can be introduced on motive, intent, that kind of thing. But again basically Rule 89(D) provides: "A Chamber may exclude evidence if its probative value substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial." And I'd just like to second what Mr. O'Sullivan said that fair trial considerations I think here outweigh the admissibility of that evidence -- I shouldn't say "the admissibility" but allow the Court not to hear that evidence if you make that determination that even if it did have probative value, the need to ensure a fair trial here is paramount. I'm mentioning one other thing, Your Honour, which is 73 bis which I'm far from an expert on. But under 73 bis obviously the Court can eventually fix the number of crime sites and reduce the number of counts charged in the indictment. And the Court has already done this with respect to three of the crime sites alleged. Now, that only refers -- 73 bis (D) only refers literally to counts charged in the indictment and a number of crime sites or incidents in the indictment. Now, I would think that a fortiori for a stronger reason the Court would have the discretion to reduce the burden of the number of incidents in this case to the -- with respect to non-charged incidents. And that's -- I think it's subsumed, non-charged incidents are subsumed within the rationale of 73 bis (D). Now, again, this is my off the cuff non-researched interpretation reached five minutes ago after listening to these arguments. But I really think it makes sense and I think that Your Honours could also refuse -- even if you decide that the evidence has the probative value Mr. Stamp says it has, that aside from the 89 -- Rule 89 reference, you could also just try exclusion of this evidence under the rationale of 73 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You might also suggest that 73 bis (D) is quite difficult to apply if you don't actually know the number of crime sites or incidents that are within the indictment. In other words, if you don't know the hidden depths of the indictment, you can't use the rule at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: The only problem of that, Your Honour, is I didn't think of it and I think you're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, we've already looked at this in our earlier deliberations this morning. Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I may have a little bit different tact than you've heard, and I hope the Chamber understands that what I'm saying to you now is really coming off the top of my head and I haven't had a chance to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, can I just interrupt you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There was another comment I wanted to make to Mr. Sepenuk which I forgot there for the moment. The problem with the fair trial point may be that you have had notice of the material that's behind this; generally speaking, it's contained in the disclosed material. So the fair trial point is confined, I think, to the question whether the particular events have to be included in the indictment. And the answer the Prosecution have given, since we came back in at 12.00 is that they do not seek a conviction based on that material alone, and therefore would suggest that it's not something that needs to be included in the indictment. I'm just trying to articulate the response to you. I'm not expressing a view to you one way or another. Is there anything else you want to say on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No, I think that's a very fair comment, Your Honour, and maybe I'm -- from the point of view from someone who's only been on the case since mid-May, I've been assiduously preparing with respect to what is charged. That's a difficult enough burden in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So have we. I hope -- or maybe that, maybe that's a mistake in trying to concentrate on what's actually specified in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Even from the point of view of working out how you're going to write a judgement in a case like this, you tend to look at the chapters that are identified in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And I think that that -- hopefully that's another factor that the Court will consider in -- ultimately in rendering its decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry, Mr. Ackerman, for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No problem. I was just -- I was trying to suggest that what I say to you today is coming pretty much off the top of my head and if I had more time to reflect I might be a little more helpful. I think we must be careful that we don't mix apples and oranges together here. And I characterise the apple as being the indictment. The indictment is that document which provides us notice of the offences which we are required to meet and the offences upon which we are potentially to be convicted if the Prosecution proves its case beyond a reasonable doubt. And I think what Mr. Stamp said earlier today indicates that the Prosecution agrees with the proposition that I stated earlier, that the -- the potential for conviction must remain within the four corners of the indictment itself, that the Prosecution can't bring -- during the course of the trial bring in a new incident and ask you to convict on it if it's not an incident that's contained within the indictment. So the indictment I would characterise as the apple that we need to be concerned about and that the Prosecution's evidence in terms of what can be used to convict these defendants must be that which is contained within the four corners of the indictment, that which is suggested by the indictment. The oranges on the other hand -- and it seems to me the Prosecution is trying to implicate some law that comes from domestic jurisdictions which would permit the proof of what we call, in America at least, extraneous crimes and in many domestic jurisdictions you can bring in evidence of these extraneous offences to the extent that they go to things like proof of intent, proof of membership in a conspiracy, things of that nature. And it's important to understand that that law arises out of primarily situations where there is a person charged with one murder or one drug offence or one discrete offence. And so these extraneous offences may help the trier of fact in dealing with issues like intent and things like that as an extraneous matter. It can have nothing to do -- the person cannot convicted of any of this evidence but it can assist the Chamber. It seems to me that that doesn't apply here, in an indictment that is as broad-based as this one where there is an opportunity contained within the four corners of this indictment for the Prosecution to show all of these extraneous things, the course of conduct, widespread and systematic, the intent, the things which could in a very limited kind of indictment maybe provide the basis for some extraneous evidence. The question it seems really comes down to just one thing: How much time does this Chamber want to spend listening to evidence that is not contained in the indictment? And will it be helpful to you? If the Prosecution can't prove their case within the four corners of such a broad-based indictment, I can't imagine us listening here for days listening to evidence that is not contained within the indictment is going to be of much assistance. As a lot of people pointed out here today, the Prosecution had an awful lot of time to decide exactly what it was they wanted to put within the four corners of the indictment and it seems that it might make sense just in terms of judicial economy that they be restricted to that. Thank you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Does anyone else wish to make any submission on the matter? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We are going to adjourn to deliberate further on this. I don't know that we'll have an answer to the question by a quarter to 2.00, but if we do have an answer fairly soon we'll relay it to the parties so that arrangements can be made for tomorrow. And once you've had a chance to consider the position, in any event we will relay a message to you what will actually happen tomorrow. Meanwhile, we'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 19th day of September, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.24 p.m.,
